mapper.verbatim_quote: the authorized officer may enter the premises and exercise in, upon and in respect of the premises all the powers referred to in section 113 in as full and ample a manner as if he were authorized to do so by a warrant issued under that section
mapper.rationale: Authorized officer may search/seize and access personal data without a warrant based on own belief, i.e. no independent judicial authorization required.

verifier.reason: Section 114 governs search-and-seizure powers when a warrant cannot be obtained due to urgency (risk of evidence tampering). Section 115 grants access to computerized data during such searches. These provisions concern investigative procedures and evidence handling in the context of PDPA enforcement — not government access to personal data held by private entities or communications providers. The "authorized officer" acts as an enforcement agent in response to suspected PDPA violations. The trap rule applies: 7.5 is government access to PERSONAL DATA without judicial authorization, not generic inspection of business records by a regulator. These provisions enable inspection of records/evidence at premises under an emergency exception to warrant requirements, which is a procedural/enforcement mechanism, not a standing, discretionary government access regime to personal data. Score 0.

escalation.reason: s.114 lets an authorized officer conduct search/seizure WITHOUT warrant (bypassing s.113's judicial warrant) on his own satisfaction of "reasonable cause," and s.115 grants access to computerized data. Personal data under PDPA is accessed with no independent judicial authorization → 7.5 fires at 1. Not merely a regulator's business-record inspection; it is government access to personal data absent a court order.

mapper.verbatim_quote: A data controller shall appoint one or more data protection officers who shall be accountable to the data controller for the compliance with this Act.
mapper.rationale: Mandatory DPO requirement applying to all data controllers (and processors) horizontally, not limited to a specific sector -> score 1.

verifier.reason: Section 12a(1)–(2) of the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024 imposes a MANDATORY duty on data controllers and data processors to appoint one or more data protection officers. The duty is horizontal (applies across all sectors under the Act's scope) and is not merely advisory. This satisfies the DPO requirement under indicator 7.4. The scoring tree branch '1' applies: "A DPO requirement (alone, or together with a DPIA requirement) applies to ALL sectors."

mapper.verbatim_quote:
the Minister may specify any place outside Malaysia if—
(a) there is in that place in force any law which is substantially similar to this Act, or that serves the same purposes as this Act; or
(b) that place ensures an adequate level of protection in relation to the processing of personal data which is at least equivalent to the level of protection afforded by this Act.
mapper.rationale: Personal data transfer permitted only to whitelisted/adequate jurisdictions or upon consent - conditional flow regime covering personal data horizontally, scores 1 per Guide p.54.

verifier.reason: Section 129(2)-(3) of Malaysia's PDPA 2010 establishes a conditional flow regime for cross-border personal-data transfer. Subsection (1) creates a default prohibition: transfer is banned unless to places "specified by the Minister." Subsections (2) and (3) then enumerate the conditions that permit transfer: (2) ministerial adequacy/equivalence determinations (adequacy conditions), and (3) data-subject consent and other contractual/operational conditions. The trap check confirms this is NOT a 6.1 ban—a compliant transfer path exists via conditions. Trap polarity verified: "prohibited unless conditions met" = 6.4, not 6.1. The regime covers personal data generally (not sector-specific), triggering the first scoring branch (1).

mapper.verbatim_quote:
This Act applies to—
(a) any person who processes; and
(b) any person who has control over or authorizes the processing of, any personal data in respect of commercial transactions.
mapper.rationale: Establishes horizontal scope of Malaysia's comprehensive PDPA 2010, controlling evidence a comprehensive framework exists (score 0, framework present).

verifier.reason: Section 2(2) is a scope-and-application provision of the PDPA 2010 itself, defining territorial and personal applicability. Per the 7.1 coding rules (Indicator Reference row 80): "Per-provision citations of a data-protection act tagged 7.1 are not discoveries and score zero." The 7.1 indicator is ECONOMY-LEVEL—it asks whether a comprehensive horizontal DP framework EXISTS at all. Individual provisions of that act are not separate discoveries. The PDPA 2010 as a whole (a comprehensive horizontal act) is the controlling evidence for 7.1 and scores 0. This section's citation alone does not advance the indicator.

escalation.reason: 7.1 is economy-level: MY PDPA 2010 is a comprehensive horizontal DP law. This scope/application provision (s.2) shows cross-sectoral applicability to any person processing personal data in commercial transactions → framework exists → 0 (inverted polarity). Not 1 despite strong law found. This is the canonical scope-provision citation for the economy-level answer.

mapper.verbatim_quote: In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires
mapper.rationale: Economy-level indicator; this is a per-provision definitions clause, not the controlling scope citation. MY Cyber Security Act 2024 is a dedicated horizontal cybersecurity law, so economy score is 0, but this individual provision is not a separate discovery.

verifier.reason: Section 4 is a definitions/interpretation section of the Cyber Security Act 2024. It provides terminology (cyber security threat, directive, national critical information infrastructure, etc.) but contains NO substantive cybersecurity-specific regulatory framework, control, or obligation. Per TRAP (economy-level, not provision-level): individual provisions of a cybersecurity act are not separate 7.2 discoveries. The 7.2 indicator requires assessment of whether a dedicated cybersecurity framework EXISTS and applies horizontally or sectorally—not citation of definitional provisions. Score determination belongs at the economy level (the Act as a whole), not per-provision. This section cannot standalone evidence 7.2.

escalation.reason: MY Cyber Security Act 2024 is a dedicated, horizontally-applicable cybersecurity framework (defining cyber security threats/incidents, CII regime, Chief Executive powers). Inverted polarity: existence of a dedicated horizontal cybersecurity law scores 0. This is the economy-level 7.2 answer; s.4 (interpretation) is being cited but the controlling scope evidence is the Act itself. Not a mere cybercrime/computer-misuse offence statute.

mapper.verbatim_quote: preserved for a period of seven years from the latest date to which the record relates
mapper.rationale: Specifies explicit minimum retention duration (7 years) for tax records, satisfying the minimum-period rule.

verifier.reason: Service Tax Act 2018 s.24(2) imposes a 7-year retention requirement on tax/business records (invoices, receipts, debit notes, credit notes, imported service records). However, this is a CORPORATE RECORD-KEEPING/TAX COMPLIANCE rule, not a personal-data retention requirement. Indicator 7.3 defines its scope as data retention mandates designed for investigative/law-enforcement purposes on personal data. The 7-year threshold here is part of general tax administration (record preservation for audits, compliance), not a minimum period of personal-data retention. TRAP CHECK: This is a DURATION rule (7 years) but applied to business/tax records held domestically. It does not evidence a personal-data retention mandate per se. Therefore, it falls outside 7.3's scope and should not be scored.

escalation.reason: s.24(2)(a) mandates records be "preserved for a period of seven years" — a specified minimum retention floor, not a max-period limitation. Records are commercial (taxable person's invoices etc.), not government data. Note: (c) local-keeping is 6.2, separate; 7.3 fires on the 7-year duration → branch 1.

mapper.verbatim_quote:
kept in Malaysia, except as otherwise approved by the
Director General and subject to such conditions as he deems fit.
mapper.rationale: Sector-specific (service tax records) local storage requirement, category (2) -> 0.5; conditional exception via DG approval doesn't negate the default local-storage mandate.

verifier.reason: Section 24(2) of the Service Tax Act 2018 is a general RECORD-KEEPING duty (preservation of tax records for 7 years and domestic location) applying to tax administration. It does not constitute a DATA LOCALIZATION measure under 6.2. TRAP CHECK: 6.2 defines "local storage requirement" as a mandate that a COPY of certain data be kept within the economy for COMMERCIAL TRANSACTIONS potentially affecting data flows. The trap-rule (Disambiguation, Guide p.51 fn.34) explicitly warns: "a duty to keep books or records, with no requirement about where they are kept, is not 6.2." Here, s.24(2)(c) requires records be "kept in Malaysia" but this is a TAX COMPLIANCE obligation on service providers, not a DATA PROTECTION or COMMERCIAL DATA-FLOW measure. The provision governs tax record retention/location for government compliance, not the transfer or storage of data relating to commercial transactions. It applies to business records (invoices, receipts) for tax purposes, not personal data or commercial data subject to transfer restrictions. Not in scope for 6.1-6.4 commercial-transaction focus.

escalation.reason: s.24(2)(c) requires records be "kept in Malaysia" (a LOCATION rule, not duration), while transfer/access abroad is possible only with DG approval. This is a local storage requirement for a specific data set (service-tax accounting records), a category-(2) sectoral measure → 0.5. The 7-year rule in (a) is separately 7.3, not 6.2. Not 6.3 (no build mandate; existing local facilities suffice).
